findings.measured: Almost no content above 16 kHz; check whether an MP3/AAC or low-passed file was used as a source.

steps.text: Check the session for MP3 or AAC files, such as samples or imported references.
Look for a low-pass filter on the master or a bus cutting everything above 16 kHz.

findings.measured: Loudness range is 1.8 LU; there is little contrast between sections.

steps.text: Press A to show automation and draw volume so verses sit 2–3 dB below choruses.

other_options.text: In Pro-C 2 on the mix bus, raise Threshold or lengthen Attack until transients come through.

notes.headline: Technically clean at 10/10 — nothing is broken, but two things are worth a quick check before you call it done: no content above 16 kHz and only 1.8 LU of loudness range.
notes.summary: This master measures clean: -17.08 LUFS integrated, -4.15 dBTP true peak, 12.9 dB peak-to-loudness, and a healthy 0.975 low-end correlation with only 0.92 dB of mono loss. Nothing here will misbehave on playback, so the score reflects that. The two flags are informational: there's almost nothing above 16 kHz, which can mean a lossy or low-passed file made it into the chain, and the loudness range of 1.84 LU says the song sits at one level from top to bottom. Both are worth ruling out rather than fixing blind.

priorities.title: Confirm nothing lossy or low-passed is in the chain
priorities.why: Almost no content above 16 kHz is normal for some material, but it's also the signature of an MP3/AAC source or a forgotten low-pass. If a lossy file slipped in, you're distributing its artifacts, and that's not recoverable later.

priorities.title: Decide whether the flat 1.8 LU is intentional
priorities.why: With a loudness range of 1.8 LU there's very little contrast between sections, so choruses won't feel like they lift. If that's the arrangement, leave it; if it's the compression, it's easy to give back.

listen_for: A/B the master against the highest-quality source stems on good headphones, listening to cymbals and vocal sibilance for the dulled or swishy top end a lossy source leaves behind.
Play the transition from verse into chorus and ask whether the chorus actually arrives louder, or just denser.
Check snare and transient attack through the loudest section — if they sound flattened, try the Pro-C 2 adjustment in F2.2 before touching automation.
Sum to mono on a single speaker and confirm the low end stays put, which the 0.975 low-end correlation predicts.
strengths: Mono compatibility is excellent: 0.975 low-end correlation and only 0.92 dB mono loss, so the low end holds up on club and phone playback.
Left/right balance is near dead center at -0.4 dB.
Plenty of peak headroom and dynamics — -4.15 dBTP true peak with 12.9 dB peak-to-loudness means no clipping or inter-sample trouble at encoding.

judge.priority_order: F1 (possible lossy source, unrecoverable) is placed before F2 (informational loudness range), matching the report's order and severity/impact weighting.
judge.explains_impact: F1's why explains distributing lossy artifacts and F2's why explains choruses won't feel like they lift, both going beyond the raw numbers.
judge.groups_causes: The two findings have unrelated causes (source quality vs. dynamic range) and are correctly kept as separate priorities rather than merged.
judge.specific: Notes reference the exact LUFS, dBTP, LRA, and correlation figures from this bounce and tie advice to specific FabFilter tools mentioned in the report.
judge.stage_appropriate: Notes treat this as a finished master (praising true peak/headroom and low-end correlation) consistent with the report's 'Release-ready' master label.
judge.faithful: All claims (measurements, findings, strengths) match the report; no contradicted or invented data.
judge.concise: Given the report already found the mix clean with only two info-level flags, the notes stay proportionate, avoiding hype while covering both findings and useful listening checks.
